Mutations causing low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) may not necessarily lead to an increase in carotid intima-media thickness. In fact, research suggests that genetic variants associated with low HDL-C may be insufficient to promote early carotid atherosclerosis.

This is because the relationship between HDL-C levels and carotid intima-media thickness is complex and influenced by multiple factors beyond just cholesterol levels. Other factors such as inflammation, smoking status, diet, and lifestyle also play important roles in determining cardiovascular risk.

In studies, selective screening of patients aged 70 years or older, with other cardiovascular risk factors (such as carotid bruit, history of cerebrovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, or peripheral vascular disease) may reduce the need for invasive carotid intima-media thickness testing. However, these results have been met with criticism, highlighting the need for further studies to evaluate the effectiveness and utility of such selective screening strategies.

In conclusion, while mutations causing low HDL-C levels may contribute to cardiovascular risk factors, they do not necessarily promote increased carotid intima-media thickness. Further research is needed to better understand the complex relationships between HDL-C levels, inflammation, and cardiovascular health.
